utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was one preliminary matter to be raised by the Prosecution. How much time would that take?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness perhaps already be prepared to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is in relation to Defence Exhibit D1061, that was admitted last Thursday and we were given an opportunity until today to revisit the admission of that document, and this is just to inform you that we have no objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it was already admitted, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we don't have to take any further action. Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Mr. Stojanovic, viva voce, one hour and a half, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gajic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Gajic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Could you move slightly away from the microphone, not too much, but just a bit. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, could you please slowly state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I am Ljubodrag Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, could you please tell the Court what you are in terms of your education?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I'm a banking clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any kind of military training and education?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the military? Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Republic of Serbia, actually the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: In Zavidovici, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you to make a little pause between question and answer so that the interpreters are better able to interpret your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live until 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: In Valjevo, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Likewise, Valjevo, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, were you in Bosnia-Herzegovina at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No, until June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in June 1995? How come you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: During the night between the 20th and the 21st of June, the police in Valjevo came to my house and they said that they needed to check some documentation related to me. They brought me in for some kind of interview, investigation interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: After that, during that night, during that morning, together with other men who had been brought in, I was taken by bus first to the building of the Ministry of the Interior in Zvornik and Dusko Jevic came there. Of course then I didn't know him. And from the people who were there -- from among the people who were there, he chose people for police formations, people who he found suitable. At that moment I was a citizen of the Republic of Serbia and a person who had regularly done his military service in Serbia, so there were no legal grounds for me to be there where I was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, when you say all of that happened at the police in Zvornik, what state is Zvornik in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Jevic carried out this selection that included you, where were you sent from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: We were sent to Mount Jahorina. That mountain is also in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time - how do I put this? - the centre, the training centre for police formations of Republika Srpska was there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time your group, and you personally, did you have any contact with the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No. No contact. We had no contact with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Court what you did at this training centre in Jahorina and how things evolved while you were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Practically from the 21st of June until the 10th of July, in the centre we carried out preparations for physical and tactical training. So we were trained in different ways, to fire from different firearms. All in all, we were trained physically and tactically, and this was carried out -- this training was carried out by instructors from the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you object? Did you ask to have your status resolved because you were not a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I protested several times because I was kept there by force. And people who were up there said that I was a deserter. Although realistically that had nothing to do with me. Basically all people who were up there were proclaimed to be deserters, and I protested on account of my status several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you given a specific task at one point in time, and did you leave the training centre at Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th of July, 1995, we were given a specific task. The unit was lined up in front of the hotel where we were and we were given the specific task to go to eastern Bosnia. At that moment we did not know where it was that we were going, but that unit that was there, that was undergoing this training, set out towards eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, to the best of your recollection, what this task was, what this assignment you were given then was? Why you were going to eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, commander of the special police brigade, he lined up the unit that morning and he said that the unit that was undergoing training until then was going out for the first time into official combat. He did not say where we were going, but he said that we were going into combat and that we were trained for that purpose during all of those days while we were there and that the unit was setting out, going into proper combat, because before that, the unit had not taken part in any kind of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't mind if I pause for a moment. I'm just waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please just do slow down a bit. To the best of your recollection, how many people set out from the Jahorina training centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I think it was between 150 and 200 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you set out? What means of transportation were used?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you arrive on that day and where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 11th of July, we arrived in the village of Bjelovac, that is close to Bratunac in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we stayed in some school that is right by the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you given a specific new task at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Early in the morning on the 12th of July, they woke us up and we boarded these buses and went out on this new specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether this task was communicated to you in writing, orally, or whether you were given any kind of specific duty in relation to this task?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: All tasks were communicated to us orally. And at that moment when we set out, none of us knew where it was that we were going. We passed the town of Bratunac. And since that was the first time ever that I was there -- actually, I was there only once. We set out towards the town of Srebrenica. Not far away from Potocari where the separation line was, between the Muslim -- or rather, Bosniak formation and the Serb forces, that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day as you were carrying out this task, was there any fighting with the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: We arrived in the early morning of the 12th of July. I think it was about 6.00 or 6.30 in the morning. And the unit was close to this yellow bridge, and that is where the unit got off the buses. And then again we were given this order orally to wait there. And after a while we went further ahead - how do I put this? - to break through these lines where the Dutch soldiers were. They were the ones who kept this separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Dutch soldiers. I want to ask you something in that regard. Do you remember whether there was any kind of clash or combat with members of the Dutch Battalion that morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No. No, the Dutch soldiers did not put up any kind of armed resistance, so there was no fighting with the members of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of orders in relation to any kind of possible fighting with members of the Dutch Battalion, and were you personally told how members of the Dutch Battalion were supposed to be treated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we were told that the Dutch soldiers would voluntarily surrender. That's what we were told, there would be no problems, and that we should treat Dutch soldiers -- I don't know what the legal term is for this. Not to treat them as soldiers in that sense but they should be treated as someone who is not going to put up any kind of resistance towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, did you actually encounter members of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where this happened and what this contact looked like -- or rather, this encounter with the members of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: On the separation line itself, there was this observation post of the Dutch Battalion. And first a tank set out and we were walking next to that tank -- well, maybe it wasn't exactly this way, but as far as I can remember, there were some barricades there and the tank went through these barricades and we were walking on the left and right next to the tank. The tank went through this barricade and then it started entering the territory that was then under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did this contact look like, the one that you spoke of just now? With the members of the Dutch Battalion, that is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: At the moment when we entered, there was no conflict situation. There was no combat. Nothing like that. And we were told that the army and police that were there should move left and right. They should take up that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have any kind of contact with the members of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: At that moment I think that Mr. Jevic told me to move right and walk up the observation post. So I went up and I encountered two soldiers of the Dutch Battalion there, so I was just told to control that particular point. It was then that I had this informal conversation with members of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did you wear at the time? Did you have any insignia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Our unit had no insignia. We had very specific green combat fatigues. Never before or after did I see such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts or was the situation unpleasant when you encountered the members of DutchBat at the observation post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. We engaged in an informal conversation since I spoke English. We simply started chatting about topics unrelated to war. They also had some magazines there, music magazines. Since I was interested in music, we started discussing different music topics, rock bands, et cetera. So a purely informal conversation that had nothing to do with the situation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What followed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: After that there was a need to establish linguistic communication, given the fact that no one else in the unit could speak English, and the Serbian forces had already entered the area. That is why communication had to be established with members of DutchBat. Mr. Jevic, who commanded the unit, asked around trying to find someone who could speak English. One of the soldiers overheard my conversation up at the observation tower with the DutchBat soldiers. He approached me then and asked me if I could speak English. I said that I had some basic knowledge of English from primary and secondary school and that I can communicate in English although not necessarily very well. He summoned me and he said: Do join us, we need you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that one of the soldiers told this to Dusko Jevic. Did you have in mind the members of the RS -- VRS or of the police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I think they were members of the police as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what you interpreted for Commander Jevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Dusko Jevic wanted to know -- well, there was a wire or a fence separating the people who were inside the factory or a factory where members of the DutchBat were from the rest. He first asked me to inquire whether there were any civilians inside the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much time passed. But in any case, Mr. Borovcanin, who was deputy commander of the special police, and Jevic, who was in command of our unit, wanted to enter the factory compound to see for themselves what the situation was like and to see whether the people there were civilians or whether there were any military units inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on that count, Your Honours, could we have P01147. For identification, it is footage V000-9266. Could we have a look at some part of the footage from 03:02 to 04:10. Your Honours, there is a transcript which is already in evidence in B/C/S. Just so that we can follow, for the transcript it is on page 39, line 12, to page 40, line 22. In the English version of the entire footage, it is the English page 44 from line 12, to page 45, line 15. If possible, I would like to view the footage 03:02.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, have you provided the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The highest? I think at the -- I think at OP Papa" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think so because we have the captions, the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "Who is the main man? Who is the highest chief in this? The main chief? "Yes? "He is talking with your general there. Our main chief. "Is there any civilian inside? Is there any civilian, women, children? "Women and children, yes? "Yes. "Yes. "How many? "I think about 4.000. "4.000. "I think about 4.000. "Is there any Muslim soldiers in the inside? "No. I can guarantee that there is no Muslim soldiers" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please stop the footage ten seconds prior to this still and keep it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little bit more so as to be able to see the participants in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The footage you just saw, is it the event you just discussed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We see two participants in a conversation on the other side of the fence. Do you understand who they are, and who are the two people seeking information from the Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: You mean on this Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: One of them is Commander Dusko Jevic, the other person is myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one moment. Was there any mention in that conversation that you can remember that some requests were made by the Serb side for the members of DutchBat to be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any requests at that moment to have the people -- the population in the DutchBat base to leave the base itself since they did not belong to DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the part you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we do so could it be checked, and I'm looking at page 12, line 6, it reads: "No, I think assure that there is no Muslim soldiers." Could that be verified later because it doesn't make much sense. It could be that it was said "I can assure," but I was quite certain about that. Meanwhile, we can proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. So let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at some point enter the facility, i.e., the UNPROFOR base or Dutch base?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who entered the facility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin did; Mr. Jevic did; Goran Markovic, who was my platoon commander; and myself. The four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you see in the facility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: We saw that there were Muslim civilians there, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view there was some mention of a figure, i.e., 400. Do you think it was correct once you entered?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I think it was correct. There were several hundred people, although I don't know how many exactly. I couldn't estimate but I would say between 350 and 500 people, so the figure of 400 is quite realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, may I briefly interrupt. Witness, when we saw the footage and heard the interpretation, at least I heard the figure of 4.000. Is that part of the communication you were participating in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, there were several hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But the question was: In the course of your conversation between Dusko Jevic and yourself and the members of DutchBat, was there a mention made of 4.000 people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can verify that later with respect to the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I wanted to ask you is this. In this second contact with the members of DutchBat and the group of people you just described, did you hear of any requests made to have the members of DutchBat disarmed or that they should be limited in terms of freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What followed during that day, if you can tell us briefly? What could you see and observe in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: We left the factory, the four people I mentioned. I don't know how much time passed. It may have been around 10.30 or 11.00 in the morning when General Mladic arrived. It wasn't at this position where the footage was taken, it was a bit further away, and he found Mr. Jevic and myself there when he arrived with his entourage. He greeted us. He asked Mr. Jevic what unit he was from and Mr. Jevic said that he was from the police forces. Mr. Mladic then commented, saying: How come it is always you guys from the police that can be found wherever something is taking place? Mr. Jevic held two Motorola radio hand-held devices, one in each hand, for communication, and Mr. Mladic asked him why he needed two Motorolas. Mr. Jevic seemed confused and fell silent. Then General Mladic told him: I hope you were not going to speak to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you have a clear idea of the area, where was this conversation taking place as opposed to, for example, the facility, the base?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: It was some 100 metres away from this location from where the footage was taken, or perhaps 150 metres. Let's say between 100 and 200 metres from that location, a bit higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did General Mladic issue any orders to Dusko Jevic that you could overhear?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No. Later on we were joined by Borovcanin, who was deputy commander of the police -- special -- police special brigade. From that location where we met him, we returned to the approximate area of the footage. As far as I remember, there was a very large oak tree there where we took shelter in the shade. Dusko Jevic was there and Borovcanin and I think Goran Markovic, who was my commander at the time, as well as some other officers who may have been members of the Bratunac or Zvornik Brigade. General Mladic talked to them briefly because they were representatives of the command structures in place at the time. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment to put a question, because this is how we do things here in this system of questioning. In what direction did the conversation develop further between General Mladic and the people you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: General Mladic said that he had issued an order to the civilian authorities of Bratunac town to provide a convoy of vehicles to transport all the population which at the time was in the base and those who later on came to an open area nearby, in order to have them evacuated from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic discuss at all any tasks that UNPROFOR members were to have in that process?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how long did General Mladic stay there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Starting from that conversation with the officers at that location, General Mladic then left to join the group of people that had assembled there. It is there that he gave that speech recorded by all Serbian media which went global, where he said that the people would be evacuated and transported to an area controlled by the ABiH side. To the best of my recollection, I think he spent an hour or an hour and a half there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The location where General Mladic talked to the people mentioned, how far is it from the location where he addressed the civilians -- the civilian population assembled there? What is the distance between the two?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Several hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you close to General Mladic when he addressed the people in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was behind him as far as I remember. Dusko Jevic was there and I stood next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you personally hear General Mladic address them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did the population take his words, and what kind of connection was established between him and the people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The people approved of his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the people want to leave? In your opinion and in terms of what you can see, because that is what you are testifying to, did those people want to leave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a good moment. I would again like to go back to P01147, which is the same footage but I'm repeating it for the transcript. It is V000-9266. And I would like us to see a part from 23:09 to 25:25. I'd like to point out again that in the B/C/S version it is the 51st page of the transcript, lines 6 through 30. In English in e-court, it is page 55, lines 4 through 28. Let us look at that piece of the footage starting at 23:09 and ending at 25:25.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "Roger. I will inform my commander. "He says that all of the people will get on buses, all these things they are doing by" -- [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to 23:40. 23:40.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ask you now, Mr. Gajic. First of all, is this the footage that you mentioned a moment ago when you were answering my previous question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We see someone here who is interpreting General Mladic's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps if we could just go back a bit, 3 or 4 seconds. If we could rewind, please. Focus now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So to the left of General Mladic there is someone who seems to be interpreting. That's what it seems like to me. Were you the person interpreting for General Mladic or was there someone next to General Mladic who was interpreting for him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: General Mladic had an official interpreter. It's this young man there. I did not interpret at all for General Mladic, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we continue, Madam Registrar has drawn my attention to the fact that P1147 is not, as we find it in the transcript, V000-9266, but rather V000-9265. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Probably the Registrar is right on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, during this address General Mladic says that: We have provided food, water, and medicine. And during this first day we are going to evacuate women, children, the elderly, and all others who wish to leave the area voluntarily. No force. During the course of that day, did you see whether food and water were brought in for this population in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Apologies for the interruption. Just so that we don't stray too far from -- from the reference, the video that was played is from, as my friend cited, V000-9266. The trial video is a compilation of four different CDs or four different videos. Chapter 1, let's say, is V000-9265, but this is the second -- this is the second video which is 9266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. We'll sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the portion about the food, water, and medication -- I'm trying to find it again. Yes, could we look at that. You said. "... during his address General Mladic says that: We have provided food, water, and medicine." Could we have a look at that again? My recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Could we then take a look at 24, from there onwards, from 24:10. I think we are going to come across it then, because I was reading out of the transcript and it would be a good thing to see this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are aware that you did not exactly quote what Mr. Mladic -- at least if we read that well. Organising something is not the same as providing something. Unless there is any translation issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record I was wish to say that I literally quoted the word: "We have secured transportation for them, we have secured -- provided water, food, medicine." Those were the words that I quoted exactly. No other intent on my part. If the English version reflects something different, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now have a third version. In the subtitles we find "organised," now you say "secured," and what you read was "provided." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat that all three times I used the same word, and I shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that later on but there is a slight difference. Please proceed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My last question had to do with that, namely, whether this food and water were provided, and you said yes. And now I wish to ask you did you see who it was that provided that and whether this was distributed to the people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes. This aid arrived from Bratunac and I think the members of the Dutch Battalion were also distributing food as far as I can remember. I don't know whether they had these dry rations or something like that. And then from Bratunac this aid arrived. I think that bread was brought in and I think that water was distributed somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During this hour, hour and a half, that General Mladic was in Potocari, did you personally notice whether General Mladic talked to any one of the representatives of UNPROFOR or the UN there on the spot?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that first day, did you see at any point in time that buses had arrived and that the transfer of the civilian population had started towards the destination that they had asked for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the transfer of the population started on the next day, on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that first day, did you have an opportunity to see whether there was any kind of separation of the military-aged population, men, from women, children, and the segments of the populations that are not combatants?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That did not happen in the zone where I was, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say it didn't happen, are you speaking about all the days while you were there or are you just talking about the first day when you were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 12th of July, specifically the first day. As far as I know, the separation started the next day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to slightly move away from the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that first day, if that is the 12th of July as you said, did you have any other specific tasks related to the stay in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I was there with Mr. Jevic and Mr. Djuric, and I helped them communicate with the members of the Dutch Battalion. There was this specific task. We can see how many people with were there. We can see it in the footage. When the aid arrived, then all of these people had to receive this aid. And then the Dutch soldiers asked me to climb up onto an APC and to pacify the masses, because they did not speak the Serbo-Croat language. And they told me to climb up onto the APC and to tell these masses of people to calm down, that the food would be distributed. That was a specific task, for instance. That is to say, I was mostly with Mr. Jevic and Mr. Djuric, who was company commander in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this footage, you had the opportunity to see that near General Mladic and the people that he is addressing is a member of the UN with a blue helmet. I wish to ask you whether you, on that first day, interpreted any kind of communication between General Mladic and this member of the UN wearing that blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. Of course, I cannot assert anything explicitly. But as far as I can remember, no, I did not interpret anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you stay in Potocari on that first day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Until the evening hours. I think that the unit was withdrawn, say, about 2000 hours in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: We returned to the base in the village of Bjelovac by the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After General Mladic was in Potocari on the 12th of July and then until 2000 hours when you left Potocari, did General Mladic reappear in Potocari at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. As I said, he was there for about an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice the direction in which he left?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think he went in the direction of the town of Srebrenica, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That night between the 12th and 13th of July, where were you personally, physically?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The police base in the village of Bjelovac by the Drina river. It was an improvised base. It wasn't really a military or police base. It was improvised. It was an elementary school and beds were brought in, and that's how it was turned into a base. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the first day, did you notice any kind of combat around Potocari, the hills surrounding the area? Is there anything characteristic that you remember that would be noteworthy now? That is to say, above these locations, above the road where you were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Before we entered, before this breakthrough, on the right-hand side -- to the right of this yellow bridge where we were waiting, there was an oldest Zis cannon, 76 millimetres, from the world war, basically. And just before we set out, he fired two or three projectiles in the opposite direction towards the houses, hills, that were perhaps 500 or 600 metres away. We don't know what -- I don't know what they wanted by doing that. And after that when we entered, I saw on the left-hand side there was some houses, two or three houses, I don't know, that were in flames in the hills, on the left-hand side. As for these moments that you showed now, this wasn't happening. So combat took place only in that period before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of time, can you tell us approximately when did that take place before General Mladic arrived in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: A few hours before he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During this first day, while you were there on that day in Potocari until 2000 hours, did you notice any kind of mistreatment or beating of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Not where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to end before the break. This night, did you spend it in Bjelovac? Were you sleeping, or did you have any other specific tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The night between the 12th and 13th, we did not have any tasks. We spent it at that base in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this would be the time for the break, and we are going to move on to the next day after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the issues about the number have been resolved and that, Mr. Stojanovic, you were right in the number you gave; that is, V000-9266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stojanovic, you are going to proceed to the next day. I have one question with respect to page 9 of today's transcript. I would kindly ask you for one clarification, Witness. When you said before you went to the scene what we have seen on the video, you said: "At that moment I think that Mr. Jevic told me to move right and walk up the observation post. So I went up and I encountered two soldiers of the Dutch Battalion there, so I was just told to control that particular point." I would kindly ask you to explain what do you mean by "control that point"? What kind of control are you obliged to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said at the beginning of my testimony, it was quite a specific situation. The soldiers of DutchBat were not standard prisoners but they could also not freely do whatever they wanted; hence, the specific situation. Perhaps under the term "control" we could understand me being there so as to make it clear to them that, in a way, the position was taken up by the Serb forces. It was a very peculiar situation that cannot be described in standard terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not a specific explanation what it means to control these people, these Dutch soldiers. Were they free to move around, to leave that particular location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could leave the location, but I was told to sort of -- well, since the observation tower was a few metres from the ground, one could observe from there. Perhaps that is why Mr. Jevic sent me up, to go and observe the situation. I can't really say specifically what he had in mind. As far as I remember, the Dutch soldiers moved about freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What -- if they were allowed to move freely, what kind of control were you given? What does it mean, "to control"? "Control" is something else than "observe."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said at the beginning, the situation was quite specific, which is difficult to explain. They remained because their equipment was still there. They didn't want to leave. And on the other hand, we were ordered to be there. So it was quite peculiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've one follow-up question. You said they could also not freely do whatever they wanted. What were they not allowed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, they could move about freely but they couldn't go just wherever they wanted and do whatever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could they take their vehicles and just move away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a problem. I personally had a problem while interpreting with commandeering a vehicle. There was a problem of that sort on the 13th when the column had left. Mr. Jevic summoned me to interpret his words, that they needed to deliver a vehicle that had to be given over to the VRS. It was a very uncomfortable situation for me. I was supposed to explain to members of the Dutch Battalion to leave the vehicle that had been issued to them. They told me they couldn't vacate the vehicle. And then Mr. Jevic told me to tell them that they have to get out, and I interpreted it as such. Then they said again that they can't leave the vehicle and that they will not. Then Mr. Jevic said that unless they left, he would have to use force and arms. It was a very frustrating situation for me. When they realised that the situation was very serious, they did get out of this white UN jeep. That is why I said that the situation was very specific, peculiar. In a way, they were free and yet they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they could take a walk but they couldn't take their vehicles, they could not move their equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For example, their personal weapons had not been taken away, but they were not allowed to use it either. So all of it was half-way, and it's very difficult to answer the Judge's question to describe the situation clearly. It was such that they were neither free nor prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also have a follow-up, sorry. Sir, when you mentioned controlling the point much earlier, you are talking about the 12th. Now, this incident that you are explaining as to why they couldn't move their vehicle you say was on the 13th. It's not quite clear what had happened on the 12th for you to take control of the point that you said you took control of. Are you able to explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I explained about the 13th, it had to do with the situation I was in, to give you an illustration. That is why I referred to this situation on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. What I'm saying is on the 12th where there was no situation of a vehicle, what was it that you were taking control of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The territory that had originally been controlled by the units of the ABiH, the Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, it's not entirely clear to me. If the same would have happened on the 12th - that is, that they wanted to move and take their vehicles, perhaps take their equipment - on the 12th, they would not have been allowed to do so either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will follow-up on Judge Orie's last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any such situations that they wanted to leave and somebody restricted their movement on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me then conclude the topic by asking you this: Were you personally ordered that if they decided to leave with a vehicle that you were supposed to stop them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll move on to the next day, the 13th of July. Please tell the Court what was your specific task on that day.

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: My specific task on the 13th of July was to evacuate the population present from the area with the assistance of vehicles such as buses and trucks that were supposed to have been provided by the civilian authorities of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when did you arrive in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: We arrived in the morning, but not too early in the day as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Had the vehicles already arrived or did you arrive before them? The vehicles to evacuate the people.

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat the end of his answer. It was unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer. You said you didn't remember exactly and what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we arrived before the vehicles, although I am not 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the location where you were, was there any pressure on the people to leave or was it their will to board the buses to take them to a different destination?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The people wanted to leave the territory voluntarily because it was an area affected by war. And as far as I know, they left the area of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that second day in Potocari, were there any UNPROFOR or UN members present?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, did you at any point see General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he passed through. I saw him but did not stop, unlike on the 12th. In any case, he was around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said he did not stop but just went through. Can you remember in which direction and where was he going?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think he was en route from Srebrenica to Bratunac. As far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that second day, i.e., the 13th of July, was any food and water provided for the population in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to observe who organised the distribution of the water and food?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The civilian authorities of Bratunac sent bread and water. I personally distributed food on that day, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that second day, the 13th, did you see if there was any separation of military-age or able-bodied men from the rest of the population in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how it developed, this separation process?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: At the moment when a column was formed comprised of trucks and buses, people started boarding the vehicles at two locations. One location was the factory and the other on the road where there were far more people than at the factory. It included the meadows nearby, near the road. At those two locations, the people started boarding the vehicles. At the moment when people approached, so, say, a family, a husband and wife, on entering a bus or a truck they were then separated. All adult males were separated from women at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were the men taken then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: There was a house called white house. The men who had been separated were then taken to the house, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you recognise any of the people in charge of the separation process?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No. The people who participated on the 12th were both members of police and military formations combined, but I didn't know most of those involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to hear why those able-bodied men were being separated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: There was some rumour. Once it was all done, I heard from some members of the Bratunac, the soldiers, that they were supposed to be taken for an exchange. That's what I heard. But at the moment as they were being separated, I didn't know what it was about. It was also a surprise to me because General Mladic had said the previous day that all would be evacuated from the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek one point of clarification. You were asked what people were in charge of the separation process. And then you said: "The people who participated on the 12th were both members of the police and military formations combined ..." And that you didn't know most of those involved in it. Now, was that any different on the 13th when the separation took place? Was it also police and army or was it anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same people who were there on the 12th were there on the 13th -- well, they were similar. I wasn't familiar with the military structures then, but they took part in it. There were also some people from the police unit I belonged to, but I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, I would just like to ask you something to clarify. When you discuss those people, could you observe if those people separated anyone on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Not on the 12th. As far as I know, at the place where I was, there was no separation. The separation process started on the 13th when the column was formed, and I could see that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the place where the process was developing on the 13th, did you at any point see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, if you'll recall, did you have to interpret any kind of communication between UNPROFOR members and the police structures you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, from time to time, but much less. Because by that time the official interpreters had arrived and there was no need for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall any such conversations and who took part? Were there any conversations with interpretation that you were present at?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: What I remember is once the separation process had been completed and the people were taken to the so-called white house, it was then that the members of DutchBat protested. They said that the area was overcrowded, that there were too many people there, and that the conditions were poor. That is what I remember. I don't remember who was there precisely because I didn't know the Dutch soldiers. I didn't know whether they were officers, soldiers, or whatnot. In any case, I do remember that they expressed their dissatisfaction with the status of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who they expressed that dissatisfaction to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me reformulate, then. Did they express their dissatisfaction to the army or the police officers -- the police COs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: To the police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to do something later, but for practical purposes I may well do it now. Could we again go back to P01147. For the transcript, it is footage V000-9267. I would like to view the footage from 07:57 to 09:05. 07:57 to 09:05.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please stop right now for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we see subtitles, we hear no text. So it's unclear who says what is found in the subtitles. Is there any way that we could also -- or is it intentionally that you didn't want to have sound included in what we see?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I would like us to hear the soundtrack as well, and I would kindly ask that we be assisted here in the courtroom so that we can hear the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then restart the footage you've shown us but now with sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pause for a second. Could we just go back a bit, 3 seconds back. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, in this video footage, 80:8:10 - I'm saying this for the record - do you recognise any of the people over there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it's 80:10, not 80:8:10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is 08:10. 08:10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what we are looking at now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see yourself in this still?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, as you describe it, where it is that you see yourself in this still?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer which was not interpreted. Where do you see yourself in this still, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the right. The very right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go on until 09:05.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "I am talking about overcrowding in that place. Where all the men are being taken, it's too crowded. They are sitting on each other. That's why I want to speak."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, is that the conversation? Has this video footage reminded you of the conversation that you spoke of a moment ago and the objections in relation to the situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to this, I think that the members of the Dutch Battalion said that too. I don't remember who the officers were who objected to the status. Believe me, I don't remember this footage at all, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you interpret anything on that day, any communication between Mr. Djuric, Mendeljev, and somebody else, some representative of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question. When this dissatisfaction was expressed, did you receive it or were you interpreting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I interpreted it. The basic thing that I do not recall is who it was that was carrying out this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't know to whom you interpreted your words --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the words spoken in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And members of the United Nations and the members of the Dutch Battalion, both expressed their dissatisfaction over the status of the people who were at the white house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, at that point in time was there exclusively presence of the police unit you were in, or were there soldiers around as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was combined, military and police structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the military would have heard those words as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to put an additional question to you. In view of your own capacity, would you interpret any words like this to any members of the military, or would you interpret this to your own superiors?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I had to do with the police officials, so as far as I know I was not interpreting this to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now in view of your last answer that had to do with the conversation between Djuric and members of UNPROFOR, I would like to use P01147 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And yet again this is from the video, V000-9267. So let us take a look at 69, line 30, B/C/S transcript, to page 70, line 5. And in the English version, it is transcript page 75, lines 21 through 26 in e-court. And could we please take a look at 05:41 to 06:10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please stop there for a moment? Thank you. For the record, can I just say that we stopped at 06:07.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you, Mr. Gajic, can you recognise anyone in this video footage?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The man whose back is turned to us is Mendeljev Djuric, the company commander in my unit. I am in the middle, and to the right is a Dutch soldier. I don't know whether he is a soldier or an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play the rest up until 06:10. It's just a few more seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You have this video footage in front of you. Djuric says: "Let us tell them to go and get them from up there. Miki! To go around and see if anybody else -- well, it's their job to collect them and get them to the buses and wait." This video footage jog your memory that these were the words of Mr. Djuric that you would have interpreted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Djuric says that you should interpret this to members of UNPROFOR, that they should go around and see if anybody else would go, and that that is their job, what did Mr. Djuric mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: He probably meant that members of the Dutch Battalion should go above the road and check whether everybody had left, whether everybody had boarded the buses. That is how I understand this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time on that day, did you have the opportunity to see that members of UNPROFOR took active part in this evacuation of the population?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. Members of the Dutch Battalion took active part. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this active participation of the members of the Dutch Battalion, how was it reflected in terms of the evacuation of the population?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, they helped in the organisation itself, because this was an enormous number of people, so that these people could get on to the buses and trucks as fast as possible. I think that you can see in this video footage that they were giving food and water. And it was an enormous number of people there and all of that had to be co-ordinated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to stay a bit away from the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're again invited to move a little bit away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to clarify a matter. We heard the name Miki in the video several times. Who is Miki?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my nickname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we still have the still before us, you are wearing, well, I would say something that seems to be blue. It looks like the colour blue. It's a flak jacket, isn't it, a blue flak jacket? So is that true? And how come you have that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: That's a police flak jacket, and we were issued with that. I think that when we arrived at the base in Bjelovac by the Drina river that they gave us these flak jackets for protection. But it's just an ordinary vest that is worn by the police underneath their shirts. It had no special purpose. I mean, I know what a real flak jacket looks like because I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question is basically whether this is the kind of vest that was worn by members of UNPROFOR or the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: It has nothing whatsoever to do with the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And I would like to end by dealing with one more topic. On this second day, did you walk up to the white house at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: No. I passed by it but I didn't enter it. I did pass by it. This house is next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In front of this house, did you see certain personal belongings or something like that, or some equipment, in front of this white house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a huge pile of things like that, and I assumed that they had belonged to the people who were separated and brought into that house. This was a huge pile of different things, bags, things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were passing by that road -- or rather, in front of the white house, did you see any passports, as personal documents belonging to a physical person, a citizen? Did you see anything like that on the road?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I did not notice anything like that. I noticed this huge pile of bags, these personal belongings that these people had probably packed when they were setting out for this evacuation. So these were their personal belongings, probably. That's what I noticed. There was this huge pile in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any point in time on that day, the 13th of July, do you remember that there was any communication between these two men that you see before you now, Mr. Djuric and this gentleman with the blue cap, a member of UNPROFOR? Do you remember that Mr. Djuric says -- or rather, that the member of the DutchBat says to Mr. Djuric something about passports or asks him something about passports on this road, and that Mr. Djuric gave him some answer in relation to these passports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to finish by asking: To the best of your recollection, how long did you stay in Potocari there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: I think until 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the evacuation over by then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: It was over before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to slow down. To the best of your recollection, when did this evacuation end?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Between 1500 hours and 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period in the afternoon in Potocari, did you perhaps see General Mladic at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The general was there on the 13th, but I don't remember really when.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about when he passed by?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, when he passed by. But I really don't remember when it was that he passed by because I just saw him. I mean, there wasn't any kind of communication or anything, so, I mean, really I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, all these people in Potocari, did they leave the area of Potocari then? Were they driven in the direction of Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Women and children? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the separated men?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: The separated men remained at the white house and around the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Potocari? Actually when you left Potocari, did these men stay in that building that you call the white house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber where it was that you went after completing this work in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: We returned to the base in Bjelovac again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to finish with the following question: Generally speaking, how long did you stay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you have announced now three times your last question. Will this be your real last question? Because I am also looking at the clock and the time you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you'll now hear the last question of Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So let us end on this note: To the best of your recollection, how long did you stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina? When did you go back home?

utterances.speaker: LJUBODRAG GAJIC
utterances.text: It was on the 22nd of July that the dispatch arrived. We were at Treskavica, at our positions there. On the 23rd of July, I was transferred to Jahorina, to the command centre. And on the 24th of July, in the morning, I returned the equipment that I had been issued with and I returned to Valjevo. I returned home on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, this was the last question that I had. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a question for clarification. When you left on the 13th, was the pile of personal belongings still there in front of the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what eventually happened to this pile of belongings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've also one or two follow-up questions. One is: You observed the evacuation and the separation, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of individuals being asked about whether they wanted to go back home or whether they wanted to board the buses or whether they wanted to stay there? Was any such questions put to those who then finally boarded the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The people were separated by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that's the separation, that is, if I understand you well, women and children from the adult men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- so if men wanted to stay with their -- with the women and the children, they were not allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those persons who were separated from women and children, were they wearing civilian clothes or military attire or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were mostly civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "mostly." What did you observe apart from civilian clothing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Almost all of them. Almost all. Or perhaps someone might have had, say, camouflage pants but the rest was civilian clothes. In any case, they were mostly civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you have not yet answered my question as to whether individuals were asked, to the extent you can recollect, whether they wanted to stay, or are -- you only talked about the separation. But by -- I mean the women and children, were they asked: Would you rather go home or stay here, or would you rather go on this bus? Were such questions asked, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions were asked. When they set out to board the buses and vehicles, they were separated suddenly. Nobody asked them anything nor could they -- could there be any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were just then -- they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the people were queueing, approaching the vehicles. And, for example, there was a family of four - the wife, a daughter, a father, and son - the wife and daughter would be allowed to board a truck and someone would take the males away to the side. So the men could not get through. And they had no time, nobody asked them anything. Your question was about that. Perhaps they could have answered something if they had been asked previously, but no one asked them anything. They were forced to obey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then the women and children were separated from the men. Were they asked: Under these circumstances would you rather stay or would you go back home? Or was there any questions asked to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I have another question for you. Have you any knowledge about people, officials, who have compiled lists of names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There is some buzz coming from a piece of equipment. Could you please speak up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I will repeat. Do you have any recollection if anybody compiled lists of names of these men sent -- separated and then accommodated in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no recollection. They were not separated selectively. All adult males were separated from the families and the women. As far as I know, there was no screening, no selection. As far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge about any lists compiled of the names? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
